messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mina, a 22-year-old South Eastern Asian call center agent, had been married only a short time when the assault happened, and the ordinary sounds of the shift floor later became tangled with what she had lived through. One night she was walking home after work when a man forced her into a secluded place and sexually assaulted her. She described the event afterward not as a single scene but as broken pieces that would not line up in order: the pressure of being trapped, flashes of movement, and one detail that returned with unsettling force, the taste in her mouth that made the memory feel strangely real and bodily rather than like something from the past. From the beginning, she found that the memory arrived more like an intrusion than a recollection, vivid in a way that ordinary daily events were not, and each return of it made her pull away from anything that might call it up. If coworkers mentioned violence, if someone tried to ask what happened, or if a television scene or conversation even brushed near the subject, she shut down, changed the topic, or left the room; she had come to believe that if she thought about it directly she would not be able to handle it. That belief hardened into a broader sense that she was inadequate, somehow too weak to bear what had happened, and that she had to stay on guard all the time because danger could come at any moment.

In the weeks and months that followed, those appraisals shaped how she moved through the world. Mina began scanning exits as soon as she entered any room or building, and in the call center she would sit with her eyes moving repeatedly between the doors, the hallway, and the people passing by in uniform or authority badges, avoiding supervisors and security staff whenever she could. Ambulances were especially potent: the sound of sirens outside the office or near her apartment would jolt her back to the assault, because emergencies had become linked in her mind with the moment when she was most helpless. Stress did the same. On crowded days at work, when calls piled up and her body felt tense, the pressure seemed to open a door to the memory, and she would find herself suddenly tasting it again, as if the past had become immediate. Those moments fed her conviction that she was not coping properly, and that if she let herself think about the event she would collapse under it. The more certain she became that she had to be on constant alert, the more she watched for signs of danger everywhere, and the more quickly she reacted to unexpected movement nearby as though someone were about to grab her.

Her efforts to manage this fear brought only temporary relief. Mina avoided reminders wherever possible, especially when other people tried to bring up the assault or even asked direct questions about why she had changed. She withdrew from conversations with her husband when he wanted her to talk, because she feared that once she started she would not be able to stop thinking about it. She also noticed herself using sexual fantasies and activities as a way to release tension, something she experienced with a mix of urgency and shame, as though it were one of the few ways she could blunt the pressure in her body without having to face the memory itself. Yet these strategies were costly. Avoiding discussion kept the event unprocessed and made the fragmented pieces return with the same force, sometimes more vividly after she had tried to push them away. The more she relied on shutting down, the more she felt inadequate for not being able to tolerate what had happened, and the stronger her sense became that she needed to keep scanning, keep bracing, keep expecting danger. In turn, that constant vigilance made ordinary cues more alarming: a uniform in the building lobby, the sudden swing of a door, an ambulance passing outside the call center, even the sight of a happy family on the street or in an advertisement could trigger a painful spike of memory and a fresh wave of dread. What should have been ordinary scenes now felt loaded with what she had lost.

Over time, the consequences spread into her daily life. At work she became tense during calls, distracted by checking the exits and startled by movement around her desk, and she found herself avoiding areas where supervisors might approach unexpectedly. At home she kept her distance from conversations that might touch on what happened, and her marriage was strained by the silence she used to protect herself. She finally sought help after a particularly stressful week at the call center, when an ambulance sounded outside the building, a coworker came up behind her too quickly, and the memory returned with such vividness that she tasted it again and was convinced she could not keep doing this alone. What brought her in was not only fear of the assault memory itself, but fear that her life had narrowed around it. Mina hoped for relief from the constant scanning, and she was most afraid that without help she would remain trapped in the same state of guard and shame, unable to trust her own mind or feel safe anywhere.
